title: Do Schools Kill Creativity?
speaker: Ken Robinson
description: Sir Ken Robinson argues that schools suppress children's natural creativity and proposes a radical rethink of education systems worldwide.
summary:
Sir Ken Robinson opens with a bold claim: schools around the world are *killing creativity*, and we don't even notice it. He argues that every education system on earth has the same hierarchy — mathematics and language arts at the top, arts at the bottom — and that this hierarchy was designed for the industrial economy of the 19th century, not the 21st century. The result is a generation of children taught that making mistakes is the worst thing you can do. Yet, Robinson argues, *if you're not prepared to be wrong, you'll never come up with anything original*. Creativity is as important as literacy, yet we treat it as an afterthought.

Robinson uses the story of Gillian Lynne — the choreographer behind Cats and Phantom of the Opera — to make his point. As a child in the 1930s, Gillian was thought to have a *learning disorder* because she couldn't sit still in class. A doctor observed her moving naturally to music and told her mother: 'She's a dancer.' Today she would likely have been medicated. Robinson's central argument is that we have a *limited conception of human intelligence*. Intelligence is diverse, dynamic, and distinct — it includes movement, music, visual thinking, and interpersonal skills, not just verbal and numerical ability.

He introduces the idea of *divergent thinking* — the ability to see multiple answers to a single question — as a critical component of creativity. Research shows that 98% of kindergartners score at genius level on divergent thinking tests. By high school, only 12% do. By adulthood, only 2%. The education process itself degrades the very capacity we most need.

Robinson calls for a *revolution in education*, not an evolution. He invokes the metaphor of the *Death Valley* desert — which burst into flower after a rare rainstorm — to argue that human talent is everywhere, lying dormant. The conditions for it to flourish have simply never been created. Key vocabulary throughout includes: *hierarchy, obsolete, stigmatised, aesthetic experience, organic, eclectic*, and *paradigm shift*. The talk ends with a vision of education that nourishes curiosity, acknowledges the diversity of human talent, and prepares children for a future we cannot predict.

title: How Great Leaders Inspire Action
speaker: Simon Sinek
description: Simon Sinek presents the 'Golden Circle' framework to explain why some leaders and companies inspire loyalty while others don't.
summary:
Simon Sinek opens with a question: *Why are some leaders and organisations more innovative, influential, and profitable than others?* He argues the answer lies not in what they do, but in *why* they do it. This is the foundation of his *Golden Circle* model — three concentric rings labelled What, How, and Why. Every organisation knows *what* they do. Some know *how* they do it. But very few know *why*.

Sinek uses Apple as his primary example. Most computer companies market themselves by leading with *what*: 'We make great computers. They're beautifully designed and easy to use. Want to buy one?' Apple, by contrast, leads with *why*: 'Everything we do challenges the status quo. We believe in thinking differently. The way we challenge the status quo is by making beautifully designed, easy-to-use products. We just happen to make computers.' The order of information matters because of *biology*, not psychology. The outer layers of the brain — the neocortex — handle rational thought and language. The inner layers — the *limbic brain* — handle feelings, loyalty, and decision-making, but have no capacity for language. When you lead with *why*, you speak directly to the limbic brain, driving gut decisions that people then rationalise.

Sinek cites the Wright Brothers versus Samuel Langley to illustrate the point. Langley had money, connections, and a team of experts. The Wright Brothers had passion and belief. Langley was chasing a *result*; the Wright Brothers were driven by *purpose*. When Wilbur and Orville Wright flew at Kitty Hawk, Langley quit the next day — because his goal had never been about changing the world.

The talk introduces *The Law of Diffusion of Innovation* — innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards — and argues that to cross the *tipping point* of mass adoption (about 15–18%), you must attract people who believe what you believe, not just people who want what you sell. Key vocabulary: *compel, manipulate, differentiate, tipping point, limbic, rational, charisma*. The closing message: people don't buy *what* you do, they buy *why* you do it.

title: The Power of Vulnerability
speaker: Brené Brown
description: Brené Brown shares her research on human connection and argues that vulnerability — not weakness — is the birthplace of creativity, belonging, and love.
summary:
Brené Brown begins by introducing herself as a *researcher-storyteller* who studies human connection — our ability to empathise, belong, and love. She describes how six years into her research, a breakdown (or, as she prefers, a *spiritual awakening*) forced her to confront the very topic she was studying: her own *vulnerability*.

Her research centred on shame — the fear of *disconnection*, the belief that something about us makes us unworthy of connection. She found one variable that separated people who had a strong sense of love and belonging from those who struggled: the people who felt worthy simply *believed they were worthy*. She called these people *wholehearted* — characterised by *courage*, *compassion*, and *connection*. Crucially, they embraced *vulnerability*. They were willing to say 'I love you first', to do something without guarantees, to invest in a relationship that might not work out.

Brown argues that vulnerability is not weakness. It is *uncertainty, risk, and emotional exposure* — and it is the *birthplace of innovation, creativity, and change*. Yet modern culture has created a *numbing* epidemic. We numb vulnerability with alcohol, food, medication, and busyness. But we cannot selectively numb emotion — when we numb the dark, we also numb joy, gratitude, and happiness.

She outlines what *wholehearted living* requires: letting go of who you think you should be, practising gratitude and joy even when it feels scary, believing you are *enough*. A society that cannot tolerate vulnerability produces children who are overburdened by competing expectations and adults who are exhausted by the performance of certainty.

Key vocabulary: *vulnerability, shame, worthiness, authenticity, empathy, wholehearted, numb, scarcity, courage*. The talk ends with a simple but radical proposition: stop controlling and predicting, and let ourselves be seen — deeply, vulnerably seen.

title: Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance
speaker: Angela Duckworth
description: Psychologist Angela Duckworth explains why talent alone doesn't predict success — and why grit is the key differentiator.
summary:
Angela Duckworth begins with a question she has studied for years: *Who succeeds, and why?* Her research began when she left a demanding consulting job to teach maths to seventh-graders in New York City. She expected the smartest students to do best — but she found that *IQ was not the only difference* between her best and worst students. Some highly talented students were *underperforming*, while students who struggled initially would *outwork everyone else*.

This led her to graduate school and a decade of studying children and adults in *challenging settings* — West Point military academy, the National Spelling Bee, schools in tough neighbourhoods, and companies. In every context, she found the same thing: the *highly successful* people were not the most talented or the most gifted. They had *grit*.

Duckworth defines *grit* as *passion and perseverance for very long-term goals*. It is having *stamina* — sticking with your future, day in and day out, not just for a week or a month but for years. Working hard to make that future a reality. Grit is living life like it's a marathon, not a sprint.

In her research at West Point, grit turned out to be a better predictor of which cadets would *survive the gruelling first summer* of training than any other measure — including leadership potential, academic performance, or physical aptitude. At the National Spelling Bee, grittier children went further in competition, independent of their natural verbal IQ.

Duckworth's most controversial finding: *talent does not make you gritty*. Data show that grit is often *inversely related* to talent measures. She is honest about the limits of her research — she does not yet know how to build grit. But she points to *growth mindset* (the belief that the ability to learn is not fixed) as the most promising approach. Key vocabulary: *perseverance, stamina, resilience, aptitude, persevere, toughness, potential, predict*. Her closing call: we need to be *gritty about getting our kids grittier*.

title: The Power of Believing That You Can Improve
speaker: Carol Dweck
description: Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck introduces the concept of 'growth mindset' and how praising effort rather than intelligence transforms learning.
summary:
Carol Dweck opens with an observation that changed her research: a teacher in Chicago decided that students who were not yet ready to pass a course would receive the grade *Not Yet* rather than a failing grade. *Not Yet* acknowledges the student is on a *learning curve* — they're on a path, not at a dead end. This small change had profound effects on student motivation and outcome.

Dweck's research explores two *mindsets*. The *fixed mindset* assumes intelligence and ability are static, carved in stone. Students with this mindset spend their energy looking smart, avoiding challenges, giving up when obstacles arise, and feeling threatened by others' success. The *growth mindset* assumes that basic qualities can be *cultivated through effort and good strategy*. Challenges become opportunities. Failure becomes information, not identity.

In a key experiment, she gave ten-year-olds a set of problems that were *slightly too hard* for them. Children with a fixed mindset said things like 'I'm not smart enough' or tried to cheat. Children with a growth mindset said things like 'I love a challenge' or 'I was hoping this would be informative.' The same difficulty produced fundamentally different responses.

Dweck's most important finding: *praising intelligence harms children*. Telling a child they are 'so smart' after an easy task makes them avoid future challenges (because failing would disprove the label). But praising *process* — effort, strategy, focus — builds resilience. Children praised for effort take on harder tasks, persist longer, and perform better over time.

She introduces the concept of *yet* as a transformative word: instead of 'I can't do this', teach students to say 'I can't do this *yet*'. Neurological research confirms that the brain forms new connections when we struggle and learn — intelligence is genuinely *expandable*. Key vocabulary: *mindset, fixed, growth, resilience, praise, potential, cultivate, engage, persist*. Her conclusion: equipping students with a growth mindset changes the trajectory of their lives.

title: The Happy Secret to Better Work
speaker: Shawn Achor
description: Happiness researcher Shawn Achor explains why positive brains perform significantly better — and offers five daily habits to rewire your brain for optimism.
summary:
Shawn Achor opens with a story from his childhood: at age seven, he convinced his five-year-old sister Amy to jump off the top bunk of their bed — and instead of getting in trouble, he managed to convince her that falling headfirst *might mean she was a unicorn*. This ability to reframe reality, he argues, is the key to happiness and success — and it's *trainable*.

Achor, who spent twelve years at Harvard studying happiness and positive psychology, challenges the core assumption of modern business and education: *if I work harder, I'll be more successful, and then I'll be happy*. This formula is *broken*, he argues, because every time we achieve a goal, we simply raise the bar. Happiness is always over the horizon. The solution is to *reverse the formula*: if we can raise our level of positivity *first*, then our brains experience what Achor calls a *happiness advantage* — our intelligence, creativity, and energy rise dramatically.

He cites research showing that doctors in a positive mindset diagnose correctly 19% faster and show almost three times more intelligence and creativity than doctors in a neutral or negative state. Students who feel happy before a maths exam perform better. Optimistic salespeople outsell pessimistic ones by 56%.

The brain at positive is *31% more productive* than at negative, neutral, or stressed. It processes more information, makes better decisions, and creates more solutions — what Achor calls *the happiness advantage*.

He offers five habits that, practised for just 21 days, can *rewire the brain* for positivity: (1) write down *3 new gratitudes* daily; (2) journal one *positive experience* in the past 24 hours; (3) *meditate* briefly; (4) perform *random acts of kindness* (send a positive email to someone); (5) *exercise*. Key vocabulary: *optimism, resilience, productivity, gratitude, neuroplasticity, mindset, rewire, advantage, formula*. The closing message: happiness is not the result of success — happiness is the *fuel* for success.

title: What Makes a Good Life? Lessons From the Longest Study on Happiness
speaker: Robert Waldinger
description: Psychiatrist Robert Waldinger shares insights from a 75-year Harvard study on adult life, revealing what truly keeps people happy and healthy.
summary:
Robert Waldinger begins with a question: *What keeps us happy and healthy as we go through life?* He directs the Harvard Study of Adult Development — one of the longest studies of adult life ever conducted. Starting in 1938, researchers tracked the lives of 724 men for 75 years, interviewing them about their work, home lives, and health every two years. Two groups were followed: Harvard College sophomores and boys from Boston's poorest neighbourhoods. The study is now following their children — over 2,000 people in total.

The clearest message from the data: *good relationships keep us happier and healthier*. Period. Three major lessons emerge:

**Lesson 1: Social connection is medicine.** Lonely people are less happy, their health declines earlier, their brains decline faster, and they die younger than people who feel connected. Being *surrounded by people* is not enough — *quality* of relationships matters. Fifty percent of participants at age 50 felt lonely.

**Lesson 2: It's the quality, not the quantity of relationships that matters.** Living in the midst of *conflict* is damaging to health — as damaging as smoking. High-conflict marriages without much affection are worse for health than divorce. Warm relationships protect the body and brain. Men at 80 who were most satisfied in their relationships showed the slowest *memory decline*.

**Lesson 3: Good relationships protect our brains.** People in relationships where they feel they can *count on the other person* in difficult times had sharper memories longer into life. Secure attachment works as a cognitive buffer against the stress of ageing.

Waldinger observes that millennials today rank *wealth and fame* as top life goals. Yet every piece of long-term data says these matter far less than *connections*. Key vocabulary: *longitudinal, isolation, conflict, secure attachment, decline, flourish, invest, sustain, wellbeing*. The conclusion: the good life is built with good relationships — not the perfect career, wealth, or fame.

title: The Danger of a Single Story
speaker: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
description: Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie explains how single stories — incomplete narratives — create misunderstanding and rob people of their dignity.
summary:
Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie opens with her own story: growing up in Nigeria, she read only British and American children's books, and so began writing stories in which all characters were white, had blue eyes, ate apples, and talked about the weather. It never occurred to her that people like herself could exist in literature. This early experience taught her something powerful: *how impressionable and vulnerable we are in the face of a story*, particularly as children.

The *single story* — an incomplete, one-dimensional narrative that represents a whole group of people — is the talk's central concept. Adichie traces how single stories are created through *power*: who tells the story, how many times, when, and from what position. The word *nkali* in Igbo roughly translates as 'to be greater than another' — power operates by telling the story of another person and making it the *definitive story*.

She shares several encounters with single stories. Her American college roommate assumed, because Adichie was African, that she would not speak English, would be unable to work a stove, and that her music would be 'tribal beats.' Adichie had herself defaulted to a single story of Mexico — catastrophe and poverty — after absorbing American news coverage before travelling there. She met a domestic worker in Nigeria named Fide, whose family she only saw through the lens of poverty until she visited their village and discovered handmade baskets of extraordinary beauty.

The consequences of single stories are serious: they rob people of *dignity*, make it difficult to recognise our common humanity, and emphasise how we are *different* rather than how we are similar. Single stories flatten complexity into stereotype.

Adichie closes with a vision of balance: stories that show Africans as complex, many-storied people — not just victims of famine and war, but also writers, scientists, lovers, and dreamers. Key vocabulary: *narrative, stereotype, impression, dignity, vulnerability, authentic, perspective, nuanced, diverse, complexity*. Her conclusion: many stories matter — *stories have been used to dispossess and malign, but stories can also be used to empower and humanise*.

title: The Puzzle of Motivation
speaker: Dan Pink
description: Dan Pink challenges traditional reward-and-punishment management theory, arguing that autonomy, mastery, and purpose are the true drivers of performance.
summary:
Dan Pink opens with a puzzle — the *candle problem* — first presented by psychologist Karl Duncker in 1945. Participants are given a candle, a box of thumbtacks, and matches, and asked to attach the candle to a wall so it doesn't drip on the table. Most people try tacking the candle directly to the wall or melting wax to attach it. The solution requires *functional fixedness* — seeing the box as a platform, not just a container. 

Researchers discovered something startling: when people were offered cash incentives to solve the problem faster, they actually *took longer* than those offered nothing. The reward *narrowed their focus* and prevented the creative insight required. Except — when the problem was made simpler (tacks outside the box, solution obvious), the incentives worked exactly as expected. *Carrots and sticks work — but only for simple, rule-based tasks.*

Pink surveys decades of behavioural science showing the same result: for tasks requiring even rudimentary cognitive skill, *higher rewards lead to worse performance*. MIT, the London School of Economics, the Federal Reserve Bank all produced research confirming this. Yet business still operates almost entirely on the *if-then reward* model ('if you do this, then you get that'), despite overwhelming evidence it doesn't work for creative, complex, 21st-century tasks.

The solution, Pink argues, is a new operating system for business built on three pillars: *autonomy* (the urge to direct our own lives), *mastery* (the desire to get better at something that matters), and *purpose* (the yearning to do what we do in service of something larger). He cites examples like Wikipedia (unpaid volunteers creating a better product than paid professionals at Encarta) and open-source software. Key vocabulary: *intrinsic motivation, extrinsic reward, autonomy, mastery, purpose, compliance, engagement, algorithm, heuristic*. His conclusion: the science confirms what we know in our hearts — people want to *make a contribution* and be directed by meaning, not just money.

title: Inside the Mind of a Master Procrastinator
speaker: Tim Urban
description: Blogger Tim Urban takes a humorous but honest look at procrastination — and why chronic delay affects not just deadlines, but how we live our lives.
summary:
Tim Urban opens by confessing to being a *master procrastinator*. He wrote his 90-page Harvard senior thesis in 72 hours. When a researcher called to say she wanted to study procrastinators, he forgot to reply for four months. He uses this self-awareness to build an entertaining but deeply honest framework for understanding procrastination.

Urban's central metaphor is two characters in the procrastinator's brain: the *Rational Decision-Maker* and the *Instant Gratification Monkey*. The Rational Decision-Maker plans sensibly, weighs long-term rewards, and knows what needs to be done. But the Monkey, who only cares about what is easy and fun *right now*, constantly hijacks control. The Monkey is not evil — it simply cannot distinguish 'right now' from the future, and it values immediate pleasure over abstract deadlines.

The *Panic Monster* — a terrifying creature who wakes up whenever a deadline is dangerously close — is the only thing the Monkey fears. For procrastinators with deadlines (work, school), the Panic Monster eventually saves them. But for procrastinators who are self-employed, or who are delaying life goals without deadlines — starting a business, exercising regularly, spending time with family — the Panic Monster *never wakes up*.

Urban shares a 'Life Calendar' — a grid of 90 rows of 52 boxes, one box per week for a 90-year life. Most of the boxes are already filled. This visual confrontation with *finite time* is the talk's most powerful moment: procrastination is not just about missing work deadlines — it's about missing your *life*.

The talk ends without a simple solution — Urban is honest that he himself hasn't solved the problem. But the insight is the point: we all have a Monkey. The question is who's driving your life right now. Key vocabulary: *procrastination, irrational, gratification, deadline, rational, anxiety, finite, prioritise, ambition, regret*.

title: The Power of Introverts
speaker: Susan Cain
description: Susan Cain argues that introverts are dramatically undervalued in a culture that prizes extroversion — and that the world loses out as a result.
summary:
Susan Cain opens with a story about summer camp: she arrived with a suitcase full of books, ready for quiet reading and discussion. Instead, counsellors led group *rah-rah* activities and rewarded the loudest, most outgoing campers. Cain stayed quiet and began to suspect that her love of solitude and books was somehow wrong. It took years to understand what was actually happening — she was an *introvert* in a culture built for *extroverts*.

Cain defines introversion not as shyness (which is fear of social judgement) but as a preference for *less stimulating environments*. Introverts think more carefully before speaking, work better alone, prefer depth over breadth in conversation, and recharge with alone time. Roughly one-third to one-half of all people are introverts — including many of history's most transformative figures: Abraham Lincoln, Gandhi, Rosa Parks, Steve Wozniak, J.K. Rowling.

Her central argument is that Western culture — particularly American culture — has become an *extrovert ideal*: school and business are structured around group work, open-plan offices, collaborative brainstorming. Yet research consistently shows that *group brainstorming* produces fewer and lower-quality ideas than individuals working alone, because social pressure, *conformity*, and the *anchoring* effect of the loudest voice suppress independent thinking. Extroversion has become *morally coded* as better — louder = wiser, more social = more competent.

Cain calls for three changes: stop designing schools and offices as *giant group projects*; go easy on *constant collaboration*; and unplug from digital distraction to access the quieter parts of the self. She reminds us that introversion is not a bug — it is one of evolution's *most powerful designs*. Key vocabulary: *introvert, extrovert, solitude, collaboration, stimulation, conformity, contemplative, temperament, assertive*. Her closing image: she opens the suitcase she brought to camp — still full of books — as a declaration that there is another way to be.

title: Your Body Language May Shape Who You Are
speaker: Amy Cuddy
description: Social psychologist Amy Cuddy shows how 'power posing' — standing in a posture of confidence — can affect testosterone and cortisol levels and change outcomes.
summary:
Amy Cuddy opens with a question: *Do our bodies change our minds, or do our minds change our bodies?* She is a social psychologist who studies how nonverbal behaviour — body language — affects not just how others see us, but how we see ourselves. Her research focuses on *power poses*: expansive, open body positions that humans and other animals assume when they feel powerful.

Her central finding: holding a *high-power pose* for just two minutes measurably changes hormone levels. Testosterone (dominance hormone) rises by about 20%. Cortisol (stress hormone) drops by about 25%. These chemical changes produce *real behavioural effects* — participants who power-posed before a simulated job interview were judged more hireable, more confident, and more engaging — not because of what they said, but because of *how they carried themselves*.

Cuddy draws on evolutionary research showing that powerful animals and humans alike expand to take up more space — *open up, not fold in*. Non-powerful or threatened individuals do the opposite: they contract, wrap their arms around themselves, make themselves small. She presents evidence that powerless body language actually makes us feel more powerless — a *feedback loop* where the body teaches the mind.

The deeply personal part of the talk: Cuddy shares that she was in a serious car accident that affected her own cognitive abilities. She was told she would never finish her Ivy League education. She *faked it* — kept showing up, kept performing confidence she didn't feel — until one day she realised she actually belonged. Her message: *fake it till you become it*. The tiny tweaks produce big changes. Before a high-stakes situation, find two minutes alone and stand in a power pose. Key vocabulary: *nonverbal, hormone, cortisol, testosterone, dominant, expansive, posture, authentic, presence, inauthenticity*.

title: The Surprising Habits of Original Thinkers
speaker: Adam Grant
description: Organisational psychologist Adam Grant reveals what distinguishes truly original thinkers — and why moderate procrastination, self-doubt, and the fear of failure are signs of creativity, not weakness.
summary:
Adam Grant opens with a confession: he almost missed investing in the company that became Warby Parker — one of the fastest-growing companies in history — because the founders seemed like *procrastinators*. They had started their company months after saying they would. This led Grant to question his own instinct that the best creators are those who start quickly and confidently. His research reveals the opposite.

*Originals* — people who create new ideas and champion them — share three surprising habits. First, they are *moderate procrastinators*. Grant found that students who procrastinated moderately (starting a task, leaving it, and returning later) were 16% more creative than those who started immediately. The unconscious mind works on the problem in the background — a process called *incubation*. He cites Martin Luther King Jr., who improvised the 'I Have a Dream' section of his speech the night before while procrastinating on his prepared text.

Second, originals are full of *self-doubt* — not about their identity, but about their ideas. They worry that their idea is not good enough, which motivates them to revise. *Imposter syndrome* — the fear of being found out as a fraud — turns out to be common among creatives and actually produces *better work* because they keep questioning and improving.

Third, originals have *lots of bad ideas alongside good ones*. The most prolific creators — Shakespeare, Mozart, Einstein — also produced many failures. The secret is *quantity*: to get one great idea, you need to generate many average ones. Originals don't have better taste or judgement; they simply *make more*.

Grant's counterintuitive conclusion for organisations: the greatest danger is not *too much* risk-taking, but *conformity* — people who care about being right rather than being right *eventually*. Key vocabulary: *original, procrastinate, incubation, imposter syndrome, prolific, conform, initiative, revision, volume*.

title: My Fight for Education and What It Means
speaker: Malala Yousafzai
description: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Malala Yousafzai shares her story of surviving an assassination attempt and her continued fight for girls' right to education.
summary:
Malala Yousafzai begins by speaking about the power of a single person — and a single voice. She tells of her childhood in the Swat Valley of Pakistan, where she grew up loving school and education. When the Taliban began to take control of the region, they banned girls from going to school. They blew up schools and intimidated communities. For Malala, the loss of education felt like losing the future itself.

At age 15, while riding a school bus home, a masked gunman boarded the bus and shot Malala in the head. She was flown to Birmingham, England for treatment and surgeries. The attack, rather than silencing her, made her *more determined*. Her recovery was described as a miracle. When she woke, she found she had become a symbol not just of her own courage, but of millions of children around the world denied their right to learn.

Malala's core argument: *one child, one teacher, one book, one pen can change the world*. Education is not a privilege — it is a *basic human right*. Yet today, 66 million girls around the world are out of school. In many countries, girls who seek education face violence, poverty, and social exclusion. The roots of this inequality lie in fear — fear of educated, empowered women who will *question and challenge* existing power structures.

She asks her audiences to imagine the potential that is *wasted* every time a girl is kept from school — doctors, engineers, teachers, leaders, thinkers who never emerge. She calls on world leaders to invest in education, provide books not bombs, and end the policies that trap girls in poverty and ignorance.

Key vocabulary: *rights, dignity, access, empowerment, discrimination, sacrifice, resilience, potential, equality, extremism*. Her closing words — 'One child, one teacher, one pen and one book can change the world. Education is the only solution' — have become one of the most quoted statements in the modern human rights movement.

title: The Best Stats You've Ever Seen
speaker: Hans Rosling
description: Global health expert Hans Rosling uses animated data to demolish common myths about the developing world and reveal surprising trends in human progress.
summary:
Hans Rosling opens by telling his medical students that they have *a worse grasp of global health than a chimpanzee* choosing random answers. They place developing countries and their health statistics in categories that are a generation out of date. His mission in this talk is to replace their mental models with data.

Using animated bubble charts (developed with his son and daughter into the software *Gapminder*), Rosling visualises global development data over 200 years. Each bubble represents a country — its size = population, x-axis = income per person, y-axis = life expectancy. In 1800, almost all countries were poor and had short lives. By 2007, the world had clearly split — but not into the 'West vs. Rest' binary that most people imagine. The majority of the world's people now live in a *middle category*, with rising incomes and rapidly improving health.

His most striking finding: the *developing world* is not a monolithic bloc of poverty. Countries like China, India, Brazil, and Indonesia have undergone economic and health transformations at speeds that make the Industrial Revolution look slow. Child mortality in Bangladesh dropped faster than it ever did in Sweden. Vietnam's health outcomes rival those of the United States despite a fraction of the income.

Rosling argues that two worlds — 'developing' and 'developed' — is a *conceptual relic* of the Cold War. The real division is internal: within countries, between urban and rural, between educated and uneducated, between the richest and poorest quintiles. The *overlap* between continents is greater than the differences between them.

His call: data *must be free*. The United Nations, the World Bank, and national statistics offices sit on oceans of public data kept behind paywalls and complex interfaces. Free, animated, accessible data could transform public understanding. Key vocabulary: *statistics, income, fertility rate, life expectancy, correlation, distribution, inequality, misconception, animation, trend*.

title: My Stroke of Insight
speaker: Jill Bolte Taylor
description: Brain scientist Jill Bolte Taylor describes experiencing a massive stroke in her left hemisphere — and the unexpected insights into consciousness and inner peace that followed.
summary:
Jill Bolte Taylor is a Harvard-trained brain scientist who specialises in severe mental illness. On the morning of December 10, 1996, she woke with a pounding pain behind her left eye and began experiencing a massive stroke — a blood clot the size of a golf ball in her left hemisphere. Over four hours, she watched her own mind deteriorate. She then spent eight years recovering. This talk is her account of what it felt like — from the inside — to lose the left side of her brain.

The left hemisphere, Taylor explains, processes information in *linear, methodical, detail-oriented* ways. It thinks in language, creates the *chattering voice* in our heads, and constructs our sense of being a *separate individual* — the 'I am' that feels distinct from everything around us. The right hemisphere processes information as *a collage of present-moment sensory experience*. It perceives energy flowing in patterns — it does not recognise solid boundaries between things.

As her left hemisphere shut down, Taylor experienced something extraordinary: *peace, expansiveness, and euphoria*. The boundary between herself and the world dissolved. She describes feeling *at one with all the energy in the universe* — not dying, but *expanding*. She lost language, lost linear thought, but gained an overwhelming sense of bliss. She was experiencing what she calls *nirvana* — a state that some people spend their entire lives trying to reach through meditation.

Her recovery took eight years, but the stroke gave her a *scientist's view from the inside of mental illness* and a profound appreciation for the right hemisphere's gifts. She argues we choose, moment to moment, which hemisphere governs our responses — and that *choosing the right hemisphere's circuits* brings compassion, creativity, and peace.

Key vocabulary: *hemisphere, stroke, neuroscience, consciousness, perception, bliss, linear, sequential, processing, boundary, interconnected, recovery*. Her closing: 'I believe the more time we spend choosing to run the deep inner peace circuitry of our right hemispheres, the more peace we will project into the world.'

title: What Explains the Rise of Humans?
speaker: Yuval Noah Harari
description: Historian Yuval Noah Harari argues that Homo sapiens dominate the planet not because of opposable thumbs or big brains, but because of the uniquely human ability to believe in shared fictions.
summary:
Yuval Noah Harari begins with a question that sounds obvious but has a surprising answer: *Why do humans rule the world?* Common answers — opposable thumbs, big brains, tool use — are unsatisfying, because Neanderthals had big brains and Homo sapiens were outcompeted by them for tens of thousands of years. The real answer, Harari argues, is *fiction*.

Humans can cooperate with complete strangers in *large numbers* — something no other animal can do. A chimpanzee band caps out at around 150 individuals before social cohesion breaks down. A colony of 100,000 ants can cooperate — but their cooperation is rigid and unchangeable. Only humans can cooperate *flexibly* in huge numbers. The secret: we can create and believe in *shared fictions*.

Harari defines fictions not as lies, but as *intersubjective realities* — things that exist only because people collectively believe in them. *Money* is a fiction. A $100 bill has no intrinsic value — it is worth something only because millions of people believe it is. *Nations* are fictions. *Human rights* are fictions. *Companies* are fictions. None of these exist in the physical world — they exist in our collective imagination. But they are *enormously powerful* precisely because they are shared.

The *Cognitive Revolution* — a change in sapiens' brains around 70,000 years ago — gave us the ability to talk about things that don't exist: to plan for the future, to imagine different scenarios, to create religions and laws and financial systems. This was the *decisive turning point* that allowed sapiens to conquer the world.

Harari ends with a warning: the same ability to create fictions that built civilisation also enables us to create *exclusionary myths* — ideologies that declare some humans less than human. Key vocabulary: *intersubjective, fiction, cooperation, cognitive, revolution, mythology, institution, abstract, collective imagination*.

title: What Separates Us From Chimpanzees?
speaker: Jane Goodall
description: Legendary primatologist Jane Goodall reflects on 45 years studying chimpanzees and what their behaviour reveals about humanity.
summary:
Jane Goodall begins with a story: in 1960, at 26, she was sent to Gombe in Tanzania to study chimpanzees in the wild — with no scientific degree, no special training, just a passion for animals and a mother who told her she could do anything she wanted. Her early discoveries shocked the scientific world. She observed chimps making and using *tools* — stripping leaves from twigs to fish termites out of mounds. When she reported this to her mentor, paleoanthropologist Louis Leakey, he replied: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.'

Goodall describes the complex social and emotional lives of chimpanzees — far richer than scientists had imagined. Chimps form *long-term family bonds*. Mothers and children have close, lasting relationships. Young chimps go through a period of dependency and learning that mirrors human childhood. Chimps experience *joy* when they play, *grief* when a family member dies (she witnessed babies die of depression after losing their mothers), and something that resembles *awe* when confronted with waterfalls — suggesting rudimentary spirituality.

She also observed *violence* — including organised inter-community warfare, infanticide, and what appeared to be deliberate cruelty. The bridge between humans and chimps is not just genetic (we share about 98.7% of DNA) but *behavioural*. What truly separates us, Goodall argues, is the *explosive development of spoken language* — the ability to teach children about things not present, to discuss the past, plan the future, and share ideas across generations.

Her final message is urgent: we are destroying the *natural world* on which all life depends. The fact that we have this sophisticated intellect and are *still* choosing short-term gain over long-term survival is the greatest paradox of our species. Key vocabulary: *primatologist, chimpanzee, intellect, empathy, aggression, adapt, ecosystem, extinction, biodiversity, conservation*.

title: Your Elusive Creative Genius
speaker: Elizabeth Gilbert
description: Author Elizabeth Gilbert explores the ancient idea of the 'genius' as an external spirit — and proposes it as a practical framework for managing the fear and pressure of creative work.
summary:
Elizabeth Gilbert, author of *Eat, Pray, Love*, opens by addressing the question everyone asks her: aren't you afraid that your next book won't live up to your last? Yes, she says — and she has been thinking about a different way to carry that fear.

She turns to ancient history. The Greeks and Romans did not believe that creativity came *from within* humans — they believed it came *through* them. A *daemon* (Greek) or *genius* (Roman) was a supernatural spirit that visited artists and helped them with their work. If the work was extraordinary, it was because the daemon was generous that day. If it was terrible, same. This externalised the pressure of creation. The artist was just a vessel — responsible for showing up, doing the work, and hoping the invisible helper would arrive.

Gilbert argues this model was *psychologically healthier* than the modern view — born in the Renaissance — that the creative person *is* the genius. This shift put the entire weight of creative responsibility on the individual human ego, which is fragile and mortal. The result: writers and artists in the modern era became famous for *mental instability*. The rates of depression and suicide among creative people are extraordinary.

She shares the story of poet Ruth Stone, who described how she could feel a poem *thundering toward her across the landscape*. She would run to the house, grab a pen, and catch it — sometimes getting only the tail of the poem, which she'd pull back from the other direction. Poems arrived; they were not manufactured.

Gilbert's practical application: if your work is brilliant, thank the daemon. If it fails, it was the daemon's fault. This separation of creative ego from creative outcome makes it *possible to keep going* without being destroyed by either success or failure. Key vocabulary: *daemon, genius, ego, vessel, collaborate, inspiration, external, irrational, muse, persevere, transcendent*.

title: Why We Have Too Few Women Leaders
speaker: Sheryl Sandberg
description: Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg examines why so few women reach the top of their fields and offers practical advice for women and organisations to close the leadership gap.
summary:
Sheryl Sandberg opens with a stark set of statistics: women make up half of the world's population but only 18% of US Congress, 9% of heads of state globally, and a small fraction of top corporate leadership. She argues this inequality is caused not only by *structural barriers* but also by *internal barriers* — the messages women receive and internalise about how they should behave.

Research shows a striking double standard: when a *man* is described as successful and powerful, people like him. When a *woman* is described the same way, people dislike her. *Competence and likability* are positively correlated for men and *negatively correlated* for women. This creates a trap: ambitious women can be competent *or* liked, but not easily both.

Sandberg offers three pieces of advice. First: *sit at the table*. Studies show women consistently underestimate their own abilities, attribute success to luck or help rather than their own skill, and sit at the side of the table rather than at the table itself. Men do the opposite. Women must *internalise* their own achievements.

Second: *make your partner a real partner*. Of all the choices a woman makes, the single most important career decision is whom she marries. An equal partnership at home is the foundation for an equal professional life. Data shows that when men take on equal domestic responsibility, women advance faster.

Third: *don't leave before you leave*. Women start pulling back from their careers the moment they think they *might* want a family — sometimes years before they actually do. Stay engaged. Keep putting your foot on the accelerator until the day you actually need to make a change. Key vocabulary: *ambition, negotiate, barrier, bias, stereotype, internalise, attribute, domestic, partnership, competence*.

title: Teachers Need Real Feedback
speaker: Bill Gates
description: Bill Gates argues that the missing ingredient in improving education is meaningful feedback for teachers — and proposes video-based observation as the solution.
summary:
Bill Gates begins with a question: *Why do some countries consistently outperform others in education?* He examined schools in Finland and South Korea — two of the world's top-performing education systems — and found one consistent theme: great teachers. Not technology, not spending, not curriculum. Teachers.

He then identifies what distinguishes great teachers from average ones: *feedback*. In virtually every profession — sports, music, medicine, law — high performers receive frequent, structured feedback that helps them improve. Teachers in most countries receive almost none. Once a teacher gets tenure, they may go their entire career without a single observation or meaningful evaluation.

Gates presents data from the *Measures of Effective Teaching* project — a Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation study that tracked 3,000 teachers over several years using multiple types of evidence: student achievement scores, classroom observations, and student surveys. The project found that *student surveys are surprisingly accurate predictors* of teacher effectiveness. Students can reliably identify whether their teacher explains things clearly, treats them with respect, and keeps them engaged.

The most powerful innovation Gates proposes: *video observation*. In the Tripod Project (part of the MET study), teachers who were filmed and then shown videos of their own teaching alongside videos of the most effective teachers made faster improvements than any other group. Seeing yourself teach is profoundly different from being told about your teaching.

Gates argues that the system as a whole — not individual teachers — needs to change. Creating a *feedback culture* in schools would raise the performance of average teachers toward the level of the best. Key vocabulary: *feedback, observation, tenure, effective, evaluation, survey, accountability, evidence, professional development, transparent*.

title: Can We Create New Senses for Humans?
speaker: David Eagleman
description: Neuroscientist David Eagleman explores the brain's remarkable ability to adapt to new inputs — and proposes that we can create entirely new human senses using technology.
summary:
David Eagleman begins by asking what it's like to be a different kind of creature — a bat navigating by sonar, a bee seeing ultraviolet light, or a platypus sensing electric fields. Every animal's *umwelt* (the German term for the subjective experience of their sensory world) is different. We assume our own experience of reality is complete, but our senses capture only a tiny slice of what exists.

The remarkable thing about the human brain, Eagleman argues, is its *plasticity* — its ability to learn to interpret *any stream of data* that flows into it. It doesn't care if the information comes from eyes, ears, or an entirely novel input. When the brain learns to extract patterns from a new data stream, that becomes *experience*.

Eagleman's team built a *vibrotactile vest* — a garment lined with vibrating motors — and fed live audio input into it. Within days, a deaf person wearing the vest could begin to feel the *pattern* of speech as vibrations across their torso, and eventually start interpreting words. The brain rewired itself to extract meaning from skin rather than ears. This is exactly how cochlear implants work — they feed electrical pulses directly into the auditory nerve, and the brain learns to hear.

He then asks a wilder question: *What if we fed people entirely new data streams they've never experienced?* His team fed a vest real-time data — stock market fluctuations, infrared vision, weather patterns, internet data — and found that the brain eventually integrates the new stream into felt experience. Humans are *not limited to five senses*. We can expand into new perceptual territories.

Key vocabulary: *perception, plasticity, adapt, sensory, stimulus, cortex, integrate, vibrotactile, interpret, umwelt, augment*. His conclusion: the brain is a *general-purpose computing device* that runs the software you give it — the possibilities for human experience are far wider than we imagine.

title: Let's Use Video to Reinvent Education
speaker: Sal Khan
description: Khan Academy founder Sal Khan shares how short YouTube videos for one cousin grew into a free education platform for 10 million students — and why it points toward a better model for schools.
summary:
Sal Khan begins by explaining how Khan Academy started: in 2004, he began tutoring his cousin Nadia in maths using Yahoo Doodle. He began posting videos on YouTube so she could pause and rewatch. Other cousins started watching, then strangers — and he started getting messages from students around the world saying that a stranger on YouTube explained things better than their own teachers. More surprising: parents were writing to say that their children were *not embarrassed* to rewatch a video five times, where they would be embarrassed to ask a teacher to repeat themselves.

This insight is central to Khan's argument: the traditional classroom has it *backwards*. In the standard model, students receive a lecture in class (in real time, with no pause or rewind), then go home and do homework (the hard part — applying what they learned — alone, without support). In the *flipped classroom* model enabled by video, students watch lectures at home (on their own time, pausing and rewinding as needed), then come to class to *do the work*, with the teacher available to help when they get stuck.

Khan shares a pilot programme in Los Altos, California, where students used Khan Academy in the classroom. Teachers could see exactly where each student was struggling — in real time, in a dashboard — and spend their time helping the specific student who needed help, rather than lecturing to the whole class. Students who grasped concepts quickly could move ahead. Students who needed more time could take it without falling behind.

His bigger vision: a world where education is *personalised, self-paced*, and decoupled from age. The idea that 30 students of the same age should move through the same content at the same speed is an *industrial-era relic*. Key vocabulary: *self-paced, mastery, lecture, dashboard, differentiated, personalise, scale, platform, foundation, engagement*.

title: The Secret Structure of Great Talks
speaker: Nancy Duarte
description: Presentation expert Nancy Duarte analyses the structure of great speeches and reveals a shape — moving between 'what is' and 'what could be' — that all transformative communicators follow.
summary:
Nancy Duarte, a presentation expert, begins by asking: *What do great communicators have in common?* She spent years analysing some of history's most influential speeches — Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream', Steve Jobs' 2007 iPhone launch, and others — and found they all follow the same hidden structure.

Duarte calls this the *sparkline*: a line that moves repeatedly between *what is* (the current reality, often uncomfortable) and *what could be* (the dream, the vision, the better world). The contrast between these two states creates the *tension that drives engagement*. Great presentations don't just state a vision — they *contrast it repeatedly* with current reality, making the audience feel the gap and want to cross it.

In King's speech, he alternated between the present reality — 'One hundred years later, the Negro is still not free' — and the dream: 'I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up.' This alternation creates an *emotional pull* that pure logical argument cannot achieve.

Duarte introduces the concept of the *mentor* in storytelling: the great communicator is not the hero of their own presentation. The *audience* is the hero — struggling with a challenge they need help with. The speaker is the mentor (like Yoda to Luke Skywalker, or Morpheus to Neo) who gives the hero what they need to succeed. Jobs understood this: Apple was not the hero. The customer — freed by a revolutionary device — was the hero.

The talk ends with the structure mapped out: *opening with what is, presenting a call to adventure (what could be), moving back and forth with evidence and emotion, ending with a picture of the new bliss*. Key vocabulary: *structure, contrast, tension, vision, narrative, audience, compelling, resonance, sparkline, transform, mentor*.

title: A Plant's-Eye View
speaker: Michael Pollan
description: Food writer Michael Pollan flips the lens on human-plant relationships and asks: who is really domesticating whom?
summary:
Michael Pollan begins with a radical thought experiment: *What if we looked at the world from the plant's point of view?* We assume that humans domesticated plants — cultivated wild grasses into wheat, bred wild apples into the Red Delicious, selected cannabis for higher THC. But what if plants *manipulated us into serving their purposes*?

Consider the apple. Wild apples are small, bitter, and hard. Yet humans spread apple cultivation across the entire world, planting billions of trees in exchange for a sweet payoff. From the apple's perspective, offering sweetness was a *brilliant evolutionary strategy* — it recruited a species with opposable thumbs to spread its seeds globally. Pollan argues that co-evolution is a *two-way street*. Bees didn't evolve to serve flowers; both evolved together. Humans didn't domesticate cannabis or tulips; we co-evolved with them.

This leads Pollan to question the *subject/object* distinction in evolution. Evolution has no direction or intention — it is a set of processes that reward what works. Plants that offered something humans needed — sweetness, beauty, intoxication, nutrition — *recruited* human labour and spread their genes. The poppy developed alkaloids that interact perfectly with human brain receptors, almost as if designed for us. Were we the ones doing the selecting, or the selected?

Pollan uses this lens to examine modern food systems, biodiversity loss, and the monoculture of agriculture. The *Irish Potato Famine* was a lesson in the danger of planting a single variety — when blight hit, 1 million people died. Biodiversity is the planet's *insurance policy*.

Key vocabulary: *domesticate, co-evolution, biodiversity, monoculture, cultivate, symbiosis, strategy, alkaloid, intoxicant, mutualism*. His conclusion: the distinction between *nature* and *culture*, wild and domesticated, may be less clear than we think.

title: The World Needs All Kinds of Minds
speaker: Temple Grandin
description: Animal scientist and autism advocate Temple Grandin argues that the spectrum of human thinking styles — visual, pattern-based, verbal — is essential to human progress.
summary:
Temple Grandin opens by describing her own childhood: she was not toilet-trained at age three, had no language until age four, and was diagnosed with *autism*. A speech therapist worked with her intensively. Her mother refused to institutionalise her. A science teacher turned her fixation on animals into structured learning. She went on to earn a PhD and become one of the world's foremost animal behaviour scientists — and she designed systems now used in *half the cattle-handling facilities in North America*.

Grandin's central argument: *the world needs different kinds of minds*. She identifies three primary thinking styles: *visual thinkers* (who think in pictures — like her), *pattern thinkers* (who see mathematical and musical structures), and *verbal thinkers* (who think in language and facts). The education system is almost entirely designed for verbal thinkers, and *systematically fails visual and pattern thinkers*.

She argues that many of history's most important innovations came from visual thinkers — people who were likely on the autism spectrum. Einstein reportedly thought in visual images, not words. Steve Jobs described thinking in design. The kinds of minds that might today be medicated into conformity were the minds that built the world. She is troubled by the over-diagnosis and over-medication of children who are simply *different kinds of thinkers* rather than disordered ones.

Grandin draws on her intimate understanding of cattle to illustrate visual thinking: she can walk into a slaughterhouse and see, in her mind, every small detail that might frighten an animal — a shadow, a reflection, a moving chain. Her designs, which seem intuitive, are actually the product of a systematically visual mind. *Hyper-specific focus is not a disability — it is a capacity.*

Key vocabulary: *autism spectrum, visual thinking, pattern thinking, fixation, diagnosis, neurodiversity, sensory, capacity, accommodate, innovation*. Her conclusion: *we need the people on the margins* — the visual thinkers, the fixated ones, the ones who see the world differently — because they are the ones who will solve problems the rest of us can't even perceive.

title: Got a Meeting? Take a Walk
speaker: Nilofer Merchant
description: Nilofer Merchant delivers a short, punchy argument for replacing sitting meetings with walking ones — and shares the science on why sitting is the new smoking.
summary:
Nilofer Merchant delivers one of TED's shortest talks — just three minutes — with a simple, actionable idea: *replace your sitting meetings with walking ones*. She opens with a striking statistic: the average American sits for *9.3 hours per day* — more than they sleep. The human body was not designed for this. Sitting has been linked to 24 diseases, including heart disease, diabetes, depression, and cancer. Research shows that *sitting is the new smoking*: people who sit for more than six hours a day are at significantly higher risk of premature death, even if they also exercise regularly.

Merchant's solution is disarmingly simple: take your one-on-one meetings outside and walk. She has taken *1,000 walking meetings* over the past two years. Walking meetings produce *better thinking*, because movement activates different parts of the brain than sitting does. They are more *honest* — without chairs and tables to hide behind, people talk more directly. They are more *efficient* — the movement creates a natural time pressure that prevents meetings from dragging.

She notes that the great thinkers of history — Aristotle, Kant, Darwin — were famous walkers. Darwin built a thinking path at his home that he walked daily. Steve Jobs was known for his walking meetings. Walking *moves the body and opens the mind*.

Merchant closes with a challenge: the next time you're about to schedule a sitting meeting, *just walk instead*. The cost is zero. The benefit is measurable. It is a small habit change that touches health, creativity, and quality of thought simultaneously. Key vocabulary: *sedentary, active, productivity, stimulate, ritual, posture, engage, habit, innovate*. A brief but energetic argument for the simplest possible upgrade to daily work life.

title: Averting the Climate Crisis
speaker: Al Gore
description: Former US Vice President Al Gore presents compelling data on climate change and argues that technological and political solutions already exist — if we choose to use them.
summary:
Al Gore opens with the question: *Is it real?* He answers immediately: yes — and the evidence is overwhelming. He presents a series of images showing glaciers retreating (Montana's Glacier National Park, once home to 150 glaciers, now has 27), polar ice caps shrinking, and sea levels rising. In each case, he presents *before and after* photographs taken decades apart — the change is visible, dramatic, and undeniable.

Gore's core argument: the climate crisis is not a political issue, it is a *moral issue*. The choice between action and inaction is not a matter of opinion or ideology — it is a matter of *arithmetic*. CO₂ levels in the atmosphere have never been higher in the 650,000 years of ice core data. The last fourteen of fifteen years have been the hottest on record. The *correlation* between CO₂ concentration and global temperature is exact and unambiguous.

He rejects the false choice between economy and environment. The *Stern Review* — a comprehensive economic analysis commissioned by the British government — found that the cost of *inaction* on climate change is far higher than the cost of action. The technologies to shift to clean energy *already exist*: wind, solar, geothermal, efficiency improvements. What is missing is *political will*.

Gore uses the history of the Montreal Protocol — the global treaty that reversed the depletion of the ozone layer — as evidence that humanity can solve global environmental problems when it decides to. The ozone layer is now recovering. The will to act politically already exists in most countries; it is being *blocked* by specific political and commercial interests.

Key vocabulary: *fossil fuel, emissions, atmosphere, concentration, glacial, treaty, renewable, sustainability, momentum, crisis, adapt, mitigate*. His concluding message: *we have everything we need — except the will*. And in America, political will is a renewable resource.

title: Violence Against Women — It's a Men's Issue
speaker: Jackson Katz
description: Anti-violence educator Jackson Katz argues that by framing violence against women as a 'women's issue', we have let men off the hook — and shows why men must take leadership on this problem.
summary:
Jackson Katz begins with a language exercise: 'John beat Mary.' In this sentence, John is the active subject — he is doing something. 'Mary was beaten by John.' John has been backgrounded. 'Mary was beaten.' John has disappeared. 'Mary is a battered woman.' Mary has become defined by what was done to her, while John has *vanished from the sentence*. This linguistic trick, Katz argues, is how societies perform the *erasure of male responsibility* in gender-based violence.

Katz makes a provocative argument: *violence against women is a men's issue, not a women's issue*. It is primarily *men* who are doing the violence. Framing it as a women's issue means women are responsible for solving it — by dressing differently, walking differently, avoiding certain places at night. This framing lets men *off the hook* entirely. What is urgently needed is *male leadership*.

He distinguishes between those who actively commit violence, those who would never do so but remain silent when peers make sexist or threatening remarks, and potential *bystanders* — the silent majority who could choose to challenge but don't. His *Mentors in Violence Prevention* program works specifically with this silent majority: training coaches, educators, and peer leaders to speak up when they hear language or behaviour that normalises violence or misogyny. Research shows that what bystanders fear most is social disapproval from their peers — the *peer silence as permission* dynamic. Breaking peer silence is the leverage point.

Katz addresses the *intersectionality* of violence: race, class, sexuality, and gender all intersect in complex ways. Men of colour, LGBTQ men, and men from lower income backgrounds face different pressures and different risks. Key vocabulary: *bystander, perpetrator, passive, complicit, accountability, gender-based, normalise, intersectional, dominant, challenge, leadership*. His conclusion: we don't need women to change the problem — we need *men with the courage to stand up*.

title: Where Good Ideas Come From
speaker: Steven Johnson
description: Author Steven Johnson traces the origins of great ideas and argues that creativity thrives not in moments of solitary genius, but in connected, collaborative, 'liquid' environments.
summary:
Steven Johnson opens with the story of the coral reef — one of the most creative, innovative environments in nature. Although the deep ocean has more space, reefs produce disproportionately more biodiversity. The reason: density. Nutrients, organisms, and information collide at the reef. Great ideas, Johnson argues, work the same way: they thrive not in isolation but in *collision*.

Johnson's central concept is the *slow hunch* — most transformative ideas don't arrive in a single flash of inspiration, but incubate over months or years as partial hunches that gradually connect with other hunches. Darwin had the essential insight of natural selection at least two years before he wrote it clearly in his notebook — he just hadn't found the right frame for it yet. The pattern is: hunch + adjacent hunch + collision = idea.

He identifies *liquid networks* — environments where ideas can freely mix and collide — as the ideal conditions for creativity. The coffee houses of the Enlightenment were liquid networks: ideas from theology, science, commerce, and politics all dissolved into each other over coffee. The early internet was a liquid network. The most innovative cities are liquid networks.

Johnson traces the history of the *Global Positioning System* (GPS) — a technology born from the collision of satellite tracking, atomic clock research, and the needs of nuclear submarines — none of which was originally designed to create GPS. *Exaptation* (borrowing a structure evolved for one purpose and adapting it for another) is one of evolution's key creative mechanisms — and a key mechanism in human innovation too.

Key vocabulary: *adjacent possible, liquid network, slow hunch, exaptation, collision, serendipity, innovation, incubate, connect, platform*. His conclusion: *the trick to having good ideas is not to sit and think harder, but to get more ideas into the same room* — whether that room is a coffee house, a laboratory, or an open-source software repository.
